# Chapter 8 Practice: The Periodic Table

*Auto-generated from the assessment guide (`assessment-support/periodic-table.md`), grouped by objective. 24 questions spanning multiple-choice, short-answer, and workout formats. Within each objective the questions run from easier to harder.*

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 1
{{sp[info] Objective 8.1a}} · *multiple-choice* An element with the configuration $[\ce{Ar}]4s^23d^7$ is best classified as

A. a representative element
B. a noble gas
C. a transition metal
D. a lanthanide
:::
::: tab Answer
**C.** The $3d$ subshell is incompletely filled (7 of 10), which is the defining feature of a transition metal. This is cobalt.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 2
{{sp[info] Objective 8.1a}} · *short answer* Classify each by category from its configuration: (a) $[\ce{Ne}]3s^23p^3$; (b) $[\ce{Kr}]5s^24d^{10}$; \(c) $[\ce{Rn}]7s^25f^3$.
:::
::: tab Answer
- **(a)** Outermost $p$ partly filled → **representative element**, Group 5A (five valence electrons). Phosphorus.
- **(b)** Both $5s$ and $4d$ complete, and the $2+$ ion would still have a full $d$ → **Group 2B**. Cadmium.
- **\(c)** $5f$ partly filled → **actinide**. Uranium.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 3
{{sp[info] Objective 8.1a}} · *short answer* How many valence electrons does each have, and what group is it in: Se, Sr, Br?
:::
::: tab Answer
For a representative element, the valence count *is* the group number.

- **Se** is $[\ce{Ar}]4s^23d^{10}4p^4$. Valence electrons are the $4s$ and $4p$ only: $2+4 = $ **6**, Group 6A. (The filled $3d$ is core, not valence.)
- **Sr** is $[\ce{Kr}]5s^2$: **2** valence electrons, Group 2A.
- **Br** is $[\ce{Ar}]4s^23d^{10}4p^5$: $2+5 = $ **7**, Group 7A.

The $d$ electrons in Se and Br are a filled inner subshell and take no part in bonding — a common trap when counting valence electrons for period 4 nonmetals.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 4
{{sp[info] Objective 8.1b}} · *workout* Write the electron configuration of $\ce{Ca^2+}$ and $\ce{P^3-}$. Are they isoelectronic?
:::
::: tab Answer
**$\ce{Ca^2+}$.** Calcium is $[\ce{Ar}]4s^2$; losing both $4s$ electrons gives $[\ce{Ar}]$ — **18 electrons**.

**$\ce{P^3-}$.** Phosphorus is $[\ce{Ne}]3s^23p^3$; gaining three completes the $3p$: $[\ce{Ne}]3s^23p^6 = [\ce{Ar}]$ — **18 electrons**.

**Yes, isoelectronic** — both have argon's configuration.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 5
{{sp[info] Objective 8.1b}} · *workout* Write the electron configuration of $\ce{Mn^2+}$ and $\ce{Mn^4+}$ ($Z=25$).
:::
::: tab Answer
Manganese is $[\ce{Ar}]4s^23d^5$. Remove from $4s$ before $3d$.

$$\ce{Mn^2+}: [\ce{Ar}]3d^5 \qquad \ce{Mn^4+}: [\ce{Ar}]3d^3$$

$\ce{Mn^2+}$'s half-filled $3d^5$ is unusually stable, which is why manganese(II) is by far its commonest oxidation state in solution.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 6
{{sp[info] Objective 8.1b}} · *short answer* Name three species isoelectronic with $\ce{Ne}$, one a cation, one an anion, and one a neutral atom other than neon.
:::
::: tab Answer
Neon has 10 electrons, so any species with 10 works.

- **Cation:** $\ce{Na+}$ (11 protons, 10 electrons). $\ce{Mg^2+}$ and $\ce{Al^3+}$ also qualify.
- **Anion:** $\ce{F-}$ (9 protons, 10 electrons). $\ce{O^2-}$ and $\ce{N^3-}$ also qualify.
- **Neutral atom:** there is none. A neutral atom with 10 electrons has 10 protons and *is* neon.

That last point is worth noticing: within an isoelectronic series there is exactly one neutral member, and everything else is an ion.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 7
{{sp[info] Objective 8.2a}} · *multiple-choice* Across a period from left to right, effective nuclear charge

A. decreases, because atoms get smaller
B. increases, because protons are added while shielding barely changes
C. stays constant, because the shell does not change
D. increases, because a new shell is added
:::
::: tab Answer
**B.** Electrons are added to the same shell, where they shield one another poorly, so each added proton raises the pull felt by the valence electrons.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 8
{{sp[info] Objective 8.2a}} · *short answer* Estimate $Z_\text{eff}$ for a valence electron in Li, B, and O, counting only core electrons as shielding.
:::
::: tab Answer
Each has the same $1s^2$ core, so subtract 2 from $Z$ in every case.

- **Li** ($Z=3$): $Z_\text{eff} \approx 3 - 2 = +1$
- **B** ($Z=5$): $Z_\text{eff} \approx 5 - 2 = +3$
- **O** ($Z=8$): $Z_\text{eff} \approx 8 - 2 = +6$

The core is identical across the whole period, so $Z_\text{eff}$ simply tracks $Z$ — which is the reason the trend across a period is so regular.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 9
{{sp[info] Objective 8.2a}} · *short answer* Arrange by increasing atomic radius: (a) O, S, Se; (b) Na, Si, Cl; \(c) K, Ca, Br.
:::
::: tab Answer
**(a) O < S < Se.** Same group, so each step down adds a shell and the atom grows.

**(b) Cl < Si < Na.** Same period, so radius falls left to right as $Z_\text{eff}$ rises. Sodium is furthest left and largest.

**\(c) Br < Ca < K.** All in period 4, so the same left-to-right rule applies: K (Group 1A) > Ca (2A) > Br (7A).
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 10
{{sp[info] Objective 8.2a}} · *short answer* Explain why atoms get larger down a group even though the nuclear charge is increasing.
:::
::: tab Answer
Two effects compete, and distance wins.

Going down a group, $Z$ increases, and $Z_\text{eff}$ increases with it — the extra protons are not fully offset by the extra shielding. On its own that would pull the atom in.

But each new period places the valence electrons in a **new shell**, substantially farther from the nucleus. That increase in distance more than compensates for the stronger pull, so the atom grows.

Saying "$Z_\text{eff}$ decreases down a group" is a common and consequential error: it would predict the ionization-energy trend backwards.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 11
{{sp[info] Objective 8.2b}} · *short answer* For each pair, which is larger: (a) Na or $\ce{Na+}$; (b) Br or $\ce{Br-}$; \(c) $\ce{Fe^2+}$ or $\ce{Fe^3+}$?
:::
::: tab Answer
**(a) Na.** Sodium is $[\ce{Ne}]3s^1$; losing that electron removes the entire third shell.

**(b) $\ce{Br-}$.** Same 35 protons, one more electron: added repulsion swells the cloud.

**\(c) $\ce{Fe^2+}$.** Same nuclear charge, more electrons than $\ce{Fe^3+}$, so larger.

The general rules: cations are always smaller than their parent atoms, anions always larger, and among ions of one element more electrons always means bigger.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 12
{{sp[info] Objective 8.2b}} · *workout* Rank $\ce{S^2-}$, $\ce{Cl-}$, $\ce{K+}$, $\ce{Ca^2+}$ by increasing radius.
:::
::: tab Answer
First confirm the series: S is $Z=16$ plus 2 electrons; Cl is 17 plus 1; K is 19 minus 1; Ca is 20 minus 2. **All have 18 electrons** — isoelectronic with argon.

With the electron count fixed, only $Z$ matters, and more protons means a tighter grip:

$$\ce{Ca^2+} < \ce{K+} < \ce{Cl-} < \ce{S^2-}$$

Note the ordering runs opposite to nuclear charge, and that anions come out larger than cations in an isoelectronic series — always, since the anion is the one with fewer protons.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 13
{{sp[info] Objective 8.3a}} · *multiple-choice* Which element has the highest first ionization energy?

A. Na
B. Mg
C. Cl
D. Ar
:::
::: tab Answer
**D.** All four are in period 3, and ionization energy rises left to right. Argon, the noble gas at the far right, holds its electrons most tightly of the four.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 14
{{sp[info] Objective 8.3a}} · *short answer* Why is the second ionization energy of sodium (4562 kJ/mol) so much larger than the first (496 kJ/mol)?
:::
::: tab Answer
Sodium is $[\ce{Ne}]3s^1$. The first electron removed is the lone $3s$ valence electron, loosely held and well shielded.

The second must come out of the **neon core** — a filled, tightly held $2p$ subshell much closer to the nucleus, with far less shielding. That is a completely different proposition, and the ninefold jump reflects it.

The location of this jump is diagnostic: one small step before it means one valence electron, so sodium is in Group 1A.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 15
{{sp[info] Objective 8.3a}} · *workout* An element has successive ionization energies (kJ/mol) of 578, 1817, 2745, 11577, 14842. What group is it in, and what ion does it form?
:::
::: tab Answer
Take ratios between consecutive values:

$$\frac{1817}{578}=3.1 \qquad \frac{2745}{1817}=1.5 \qquad \frac{11577}{2745}=4.2 \qquad \frac{14842}{11577}=1.3$$

The largest jump is at $IE_4$, so the first **three** electrons are valence electrons and the fourth breaches the core.

**Group 3A**, forming a **$3+$ ion**. (These are aluminum's values.)

Note the ratio at $IE_2$ is 3.1, which is sizeable but not the largest — comparing ratios rather than differences is what keeps this from misleading you.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 16
{{sp[info] Objective 8.3a}} · *short answer* Explain the two dips in the period-2 ionization-energy trend, at Be→B and at N→O.
:::
::: tab Answer
Both come from electron configuration rather than from $Z_\text{eff}$.

**Be → B.** Beryllium is $[\ce{He}]2s^2$; boron is $[\ce{He}]2s^22p^1$. Boron's outermost electron sits in a higher-energy $2p$ orbital, partly shielded by the filled $2s$ beneath it, so it is easier to remove despite boron's larger nuclear charge.

**N → O.** Nitrogen is $2p^3$ — a half-filled subshell with one electron in each orbital and no pairing repulsion, an unusually stable arrangement. Oxygen is $2p^4$, so one orbital holds a pair. Removing that paired electron relieves the repulsion, so it costs less than the trend predicts.

Both dips repeat in period 3 at Mg→Al and P→S, for the same two reasons.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 17
{{sp[info] Objective 8.3b}} · *short answer* Why do the noble gases have electron affinities near zero or negative?
:::
::: tab Answer
A noble gas has a complete $ns^2np^6$ outer shell with no vacancy. An added electron cannot join that shell; it would have to begin a new one, farther from the nucleus and shielded by everything beneath it.

Rather than releasing energy, that process costs energy — so the electron affinity is near zero or negative, and noble gases form no stable anions.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 18
{{sp[info] Objective 8.3b}} · *short answer* Which of each pair has the greater electron affinity: (a) O or F; (b) F or Cl; \(c) Mg or S?
:::
::: tab Answer
**(a) F.** Same period; electron affinity rises left to right, and fluorine needs only one electron to complete its shell.

**(b) Cl**, narrowly. The general trend predicts F, but fluorine's $2p$ subshell is so small and crowded that adding an electron there brings extra repulsion. Chlorine has the largest electron affinity of any element.

**\(c) S.** Sulfur is a nonmetal near the right of period 3; magnesium is a metal near the left and would far rather lose two electrons than gain any.

Part (b) is the standard exception. Electron affinity is a less regular trend than ionization energy, and this pair is the case usually asked about.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 19
{{sp[info] Objective 8.4a}} · *short answer* Why are the alkali metals never found uncombined in nature?
:::
::: tab Answer
They have the **lowest ionization energies of any elements**. A single valence electron, well shielded and far from the nucleus, is removed with very little energy — so alkali metals give it up to almost anything available.

In practice they react with water, oxygen, and even nitrogen. Any exposed sample combines within moments, which is why they are stored under oil and why they occur naturally only as compounds.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 20
{{sp[info] Objective 8.4a}} · *short answer* Predict which is more reactive and justify with a trend: (a) K or Na as metals; (b) Cl or Br as nonmetals.
:::
::: tab Answer
**(a) K.** Metallic reactivity is willingness to *lose* an electron, so it runs opposite to ionization energy. IE falls down a group, so potassium gives up its valence electron more readily than sodium.

**(b) Cl.** Nonmetal reactivity is willingness to *gain* an electron, so it tracks electron affinity, which also falls down a group. Chlorine is therefore more reactive than bromine.

The two answers run in opposite directions down the table — metals become more reactive downward, nonmetals less — and both follow from the same underlying trend.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 21
{{sp[info] Objective 8.4a}} · *short answer* What is a diagonal relationship, and which three pairs are the classic examples?
:::
::: tab Answer
A **diagonal relationship** is a similarity between an element and the one diagonally below and to its right, despite being in different groups and periods.

The three classic pairs are **Li–Mg**, **Be–Al**, and **B–Si**.

The cause is charge density. Moving right increases charge and shrinks the ion; moving down decreases charge density. Along a diagonal the two effects roughly cancel, leaving the two ions with similar charge packed into similar volume — and charge density is what governs how strongly a cation polarizes its surroundings.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 22
{{sp[info] Objective 8.4b}} · *short answer* Classify as basic, acidic, or amphoteric: $\ce{Na2O}$, $\ce{SO3}$, $\ce{Al2O3}$, $\ce{MgO}$.
:::
::: tab Answer
- **$\ce{Na2O}$** — Group 1A metal: **basic**.
- **$\ce{SO3}$** — nonmetal: **acidic**.
- **$\ce{Al2O3}$** — the boundary case: **amphoteric**, reacting with both acids and bases.
- **$\ce{MgO}$** — Group 2A metal: **basic**.

The single rule: metal oxide → basic, nonmetal oxide → acidic, with $\ce{Al2O3}$ as the memorized exception on the boundary.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 23
{{sp[info] Objective 8.4b}} · *short answer* Why do the melting points of the period-3 oxides fall so sharply from $\ce{MgO}$ to $\ce{SO3}$?
:::
::: tab Answer
Because the *structure* changes, not merely the composition.

$\ce{MgO}$ is **ionic** — a lattice of $\ce{Mg^2+}$ and $\ce{O^2-}$ held by strong electrostatic attraction throughout the solid. Melting it means overcoming that entire lattice, so it melts around 2850 °C.

$\ce{SiO2}$ in between is a **covalent network**: no ions, but every atom bonded into one continuous three-dimensional structure, so it still melts above 1600 °C.

$\ce{SO3}$ is made of **small discrete molecules** with only weak attractions between them. Melting requires separating molecules, not breaking bonds, so it melts at 17 °C.

The trend tracks metallic character: ionic on the metal side, molecular on the nonmetal side, network at the metalloid boundary.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 24
{{sp[info] Objective 8.4b}} · *short answer* $\ce{Al2O3}$ reacts with both $\ce{HCl}$ and $\ce{NaOH}$. What does this tell you about aluminum's position in the periodic table, and name one other amphoteric oxide.
:::
::: tab Answer
It places aluminum **on the metal/nonmetal boundary**. Its oxide is basic enough to neutralize an acid and acidic enough to neutralize a base, which is exactly what you would expect of an element whose metallic character is intermediate.

$\ce{ZnO}$ is another common amphoteric oxide, and $\ce{PbO}$ is a third — both from metals sitting near the same boundary region.

The general point: an oxide's acid–base character is a continuous property tracking metallic character, and amphoteric oxides mark where the continuum crosses over.
:::
::::
